Why shoulder seasons are a marketing problem

Slow spring and fall weeks feel like a demand problem. Usually they are a planning problem that marketing can solve months ahead.

The pattern everyone knows

Every service trade has its rhythm. HVAC companies are flat out in the first heat wave and the first cold snap, then watch the board go quiet in between. Roofers ride storm seasons. Plumbers see spikes with freezes. The quiet weeks are not a surprise, yet many businesses treat them like one every year.

The result is a familiar scramble: technicians sitting idle, a rushed promotion, a discount that trains customers to wait, and a burst of ad spend that arrives just as the busy season starts again.

“If you can circle the slow weeks on a calendar, you can plan for them.”

Why it is a marketing problem, not just an operations one

Operations can stretch the schedule, move crews or bring forward maintenance. But the only lever that creates new work in a quiet month is demand, and demand has a lead time. The homeowner who books a replacement in April usually started thinking about it in February.

That means the marketing for a shoulder season has to start well before it. If campaigns only switch on when the board is empty, they are already late.

Build the off-peak pipeline

Work backwards from the quiet weeks. For each one, ask what kind of job you’d like to sell, who is most likely to buy it, and when they make that decision.

  • Maintenance and tune-ups. Easy to schedule, good for retention, and a natural way to find replacement opportunities.
  • Planned replacements. Customers who know their system is ageing and would rather not wait for it to fail.
  • Financing offers. A clear monthly payment can turn “next year” into “this month”.
  • Commercial service agreements. Property managers plan budgets ahead and value reliability.
Example planning calendar for a spring shoulder season
Weeks beforeActivity
10Pick the offers and the customer lists you will use
8Brief creative, update landing pages and booking scripts
6Start email and direct mail to past customers
4Turn on paid search and social for planned work
0Shoulder season starts: book from a full pipeline

Use the list you already have

Past customers are the cheapest audience you will ever market to. They know you, they have your number and many of them have equipment that will need attention. A short, useful email (“here’s what to check before summer”) often does more than a broad ad campaign.

In practice · Plumbing

A spring drain-and-water-heater check offered only to customers from the past two years, booked into the slowest weeks first.

Match the message to the season

Peak-season messaging is about speed and availability: we can be there today. Shoulder-season messaging is about planning and value: get it done before the rush, at a time that suits you. Running the same ads all year misses that shift, and usually means paying peak prices for clicks that want an emergency you can’t offer that week.

Landing pages should change with the message. A page built for “no heat tonight” won’t convert a homeowner who is calmly comparing replacement options. Give planned-work visitors what they need to decide: options, financing, timelines and proof that you show up when you say you will.

Don’t cut the budget to zero

It is tempting to switch everything off when demand is low. But brand searches, reviews and remarketing audiences all decay when nothing is running. When the next busy season arrives, you pay more to rebuild what you paused. A lower, steady baseline usually beats a stop-start pattern.

What to do this month

  1. Mark last year’s three slowest weeks on this year’s calendar.
  2. Choose one offer per slow window and write down who it is for.
  3. Count back eight weeks and put the campaign start dates in the calendar.
  4. Segment past customers so the first email can go out on time.

Key takeaways

  • Shoulder seasons are predictable, so the response can be planned.
  • The pipeline for a slow month is built six to ten weeks before it starts.
  • Maintenance, financing and planned replacements are the natural off-peak offers.
  • Cutting all spend in slow months makes the next slow month worse.
